## Characteristic Functions

The characteristic function of a [[random-variables|random variable]] is its
[[fourier-transform]], viewed as a function of frequency. It exists for every
random variable, determines the distribution uniquely, turns sums of
independent random variables into products, and is the standard tool for
proving limit theorems such as the [[central-limit-theorem]]. It plays the role
of the moment generating function in [[generating-functions]], without needing
the moments to exist.

## Definition

:::{.definition data-title="Characteristic Function"}

Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable. Its **characteristic function** is

$$
\varphi_X(t):=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{itX}\right]=\mathbb{E}[\cos(tX)]
+i\,\mathbb{E}[\sin(tX)],\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

For a random vector $X\in\mathbb{R}^d$ the definition is
$\varphi_X(t):=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{i\langle t,X\rangle}\right]$ for
$t\in\mathbb{R}^d$.

:::

Since $|e^{itX}|=1$ the [[expectation]] always exists, which is the advantage
over the moment generating function $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]$.

If $X$ has density $p_X$ then

$$
\varphi_X(t)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty p_X(x)e^{itx}\,dx=\hat{p}_X(-t),
$$

where $\hat{p}_X$ is the [[fourier-transform]] with the convention
$\hat{f}(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-i\xi x}\,dx$. More generally, $\varphi_X$ is the
Fourier transform of the law of $X$ (up to the sign of the argument), which
also covers discrete and singular distributions.

## Basic Properties

:::{.proposition data-title="Properties of the Characteristic Function"}

Let $X$ be a random variable with characteristic function $\varphi_X$. Then

1. $\varphi_X(0)=1$ and $|\varphi_X(t)|\leq 1$ for all $t$.
2. $\varphi_X$ is uniformly continuous.
3. $\varphi_X(-t)=\overline{\varphi_X(t)}$, so $\varphi_X$ is real if and only
   if the law of $X$ is symmetric.
4. For $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$.
5. If $X,Y$ are independent then $\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=\varphi_X(t)\varphi_Y(t)$.

:::

:::{.proof}
Parts 1 and 3 are immediate from the definition. For part 2,
$|\varphi_X(t+h)-\varphi_X(t)|\leq\mathbb{E}|e^{ihX}-1|$, which does not depend
on $t$ and tends to $0$ as $h\to 0$ by the [[dominated-convergence-theorem]].
Part 4 is the substitution $e^{it(aX+b)}=e^{itb}e^{i(at)X}$. For part 5,
independence gives

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{it(X+Y)}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{itX}\right]
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{itY}\right].
$$
:::

Part 5 is the convolution theorem in disguise: the density of $X+Y$ is the
[[convolution]] $p_X*p_Y$, and the Fourier transform maps convolution to
multiplication.

## Uniqueness and Inversion

:::{.theorem data-title="Uniqueness"}

If $X$ and $Y$ are random variables with $\varphi_X=\varphi_Y$, then $X$ and
$Y$ have the same distribution.

:::

This is why characteristic functions can be used to identify distributions: to
show $S\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ it is enough to show that $\varphi_S$ is
the characteristic function of that distribution.

:::{.theorem data-title="Inversion Formulas"}

Let $X$ be a random variable with characteristic function $\varphi_X$.

1. If $\varphi_X\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ then $X$ has a bounded continuous density
   given by

   $$
   p_X(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-itx}\varphi_X(t)\,dt.
   $$

2. (Gil-Pelaez) At every point $x$ where the distribution function of $X$ is
   continuous,

   $$
   \mathbb{P}(X\leq x)=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^\infty
   \frac{\operatorname{Im}\left(e^{-itx}\varphi_X(t)\right)}{t}\,dt.
   $$

:::

Part 1 is the Fourier inversion theorem from [[fourier-transform]]. Part 2
needs no integrability assumption on $\varphi_X$, and is the version used for
numerical work.

## Moments

:::{.theorem data-title="Moments from the Characteristic Function"}

If $\mathbb{E}|X|^n<\infty$ then $\varphi_X$ is $n$ times continuously
differentiable and

$$
\varphi_X^{(k)}(0)=i^k\,\mathbb{E}\left[X^k\right],\qquad k=0,\dots,n.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
Differentiating under the expectation gives
$\varphi_X^{(k)}(t)=\mathbb{E}\left[(iX)^ke^{itX}\right]$. This is justified by
the dominated-convergence theorem, since $|(iX)^ke^{itX}|=|X|^k$ is integrable
for $k\leq n$. Evaluating at $t=0$ gives the result.
:::

The converse is false in general: smoothness of $\varphi_X$ at $0$ does not
give finite moments of every order. In the other direction, a distribution with
no moments can still have a characteristic function, as the Cauchy
distribution shows below.

## Continuity Theorem

:::{.theorem data-title="Lévy Continuity Theorem"}

Let $X_n$ be random variables with characteristic functions $\varphi_n$.

1. If $X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{D}}{\to}X$ then $\varphi_n(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for
   every $t$.
2. If $\varphi_n(t)\to g(t)$ for every $t$ and $g$ is continuous at $0$, then
   $g$ is the characteristic function of a random variable $X$ and
   $X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{D}}{\to}X$.

:::

Convergence of characteristic functions is therefore equivalent to
[[convergence-in-law]]. This is the [[continuity-theorem]] used to prove the
[[central-limit-theorem]]: for independent identically distributed
$X_j$ with mean $0$ and variance $1$, property 5 and property 4 give

$$
\varphi_{n^{-1/2}\sum_{j\leq n}X_j}(t)=\varphi_{X_1}\left(\tfrac{t}{\sqrt{n}}
\right)^n\to e^{-t^2/2},
$$

which is the characteristic function of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$.

## Examples

| Distribution                        | Characteristic function $\varphi_X(t)$ |
|:------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
| Bernoulli($p$)                      | $1-p+pe^{it}$                          |
| Poisson($\lambda$)                  | $\exp\left(\lambda(e^{it}-1)\right)$   |
| Uniform on $[0,1]$                  | $\frac{e^{it}-1}{it}$                  |
| [[exponential-distribution]]($\lambda$) | $\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-it}$       |
| [[normal-distribution]] $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | $e^{i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2}$ |
| [[cauchy-distribution]] (standard)  | $e^{-|t|}$                             |

:::{.example data-title="Sums of Independent Normals"}

Let $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$ and $Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,
\sigma_2^2)$ be independent. By property 5,

$$
\varphi_{X+Y}(t)=e^{i\mu_1t-\sigma_1^2t^2/2}e^{i\mu_2t-\sigma_2^2t^2/2}
=e^{i(\mu_1+\mu_2)t-(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2/2},
$$

so by uniqueness $X+Y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$. This
avoids computing a convolution integral.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Cauchy Distribution"}

The standard Cauchy distribution has density $p(x)=\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}$ and
characteristic function $e^{-|t|}$, so $\varphi$ is not differentiable at $0$.
This matches the fact that the Cauchy distribution has no mean. If
$X_1,\dots,X_n$ are independent standard Cauchy then

$$
\varphi_{\bar{X}_n}(t)=\left(e^{-|t|/n}\right)^n=e^{-|t|},
$$

so the sample mean $\bar{X}_n$ is again standard Cauchy, and the law of large
numbers fails.

:::

## Application to Option Pricing

In the [[heston-model]] the density of $\log S_T$ is not known in closed form,
but its characteristic function is, because the dynamics are affine in the
variance process. The risk-neutral price of a European option is then
computed from $\varphi_{\log S_T}$ using the inversion formulas above, which
replaces a PDE solve with a one-dimensional numerical integral. See
[[stochastic-volatility-model]].

> *Note:* The characteristic function exists for every distribution, but the
> moment generating function $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]$ may be infinite for all
> $t\neq 0$. The price for this generality is complex values, and the
> conditions in the inversion theorem.
